covers.quote: Content creators will adapt their narrative to the:
genre
users
format – for example, text, video, audio, games, presentations
complexity and scope of the content.
Choose an appropriate type of narrative structure

rules.specification: The page identifies the dimensions of suitability but does not specify which structural choices suit particular genres, users, formats or levels of complexity. Assessment needs that context.
rules.violation_condition: A narrative uses a structure unsuited to its genre, intended users, format, or the complexity and scope of its content.
when: Applies to content using narrative structure.
Assess suitability against the genre, users, format, and complexity and scope of the content.
rules.why: G-2 combines the dimensions of adaptation into one suitability check; G-4 absorbs the broader instruction to choose an appropriate structure.

covers.quote: Government content must be evidence-based
And never include any information based on an assumption that something happened because of something else.
Without supporting evidence, any assertions you make about cause and effect will result in a biased narrative.

rules.quote: So, it’s important to ensure your narrative is based on evidence from authoritative sources or actual events.
rules.specification: This requires an evidential basis, not necessarily an inline citation for every assertion. Establishing the basis and authority of evidence may require material outside the narrative.
rules.violation_condition: Factual or cause-and-effect assertions in a narrative lack a basis in authoritative evidence or actual events, including causal assertions based only on an assumption.
when: Applies to government narratives.
A believable story is not itself supporting evidence.
Cause-and-effect assertions require supporting evidence; an assumption that one event caused another is insufficient.
rules.why: G-2 treats unsupported causal claims as a case of the evidential-support check; G-4 combines the repeated statements of that obligation.

rules.quote: Don’t include details that might work with the story but aren’t factual.
rules.violation_condition: A government narrative includes non-factual details to make the story work.
when: Applies to details presented as factual in government narratives.
A detail’s usefulness to the story does not justify its being non-factual.
rules.why: The rule-grain test distinguishes a false detail from a claim whose evidential basis is missing; these are different reasons for a finding.

covers.quote: A combination of narrative structures can work, depending on the content’s purpose and its format.

rules.quote: Simple structures are best for government writing.
rules.specification: The page prefers simple structures but gives no complexity threshold. It does not prohibit combining structures when the content’s purpose and format warrant it.
rules.violation_condition: A government narrative uses an unnecessarily complex structure where a simple structure would serve its purpose and format.
when: Applies to government writing using narrative structure.
A combination of narrative structures can be appropriate depending on the content’s purpose and format.
rules.why: G-3 records the permission to combine structures as a qualification, not a separate rule.

covers.quote: Use narrative structure to tell a story
All types of narrative structure, including linear, follow a consistent pattern: they have a beginning, middle and end.
While the order of the sequence usually remains the same, elements of the 3 parts will vary depending on the type of content.
Narrative structure starts with an introduction (‘exposition’ or ‘set-up’).
The middle (‘rising action’ or ‘plot progression’) gives users more detail.
Narrative structure has a conclusion (‘resolution’ or ‘falling action’).

rules.quote: Write a beginning, middle and end
rules.violation_condition: Narrative content lacks a beginning, a middle or an end.
when: Applies to content using narrative structure.
The elements of each part vary with the type and format of content.
The parts are structural functions, not a requirement for headings literally named Beginning, Middle and End.
The listed uses of each part are genre-dependent possibilities, not a checklist required in every narrative.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the general storytelling instruction with its explicit structural requirement. This heading states a presence check; the child sections largely describe possible functions rather than separate mandatory components.

rules.quote: Users shouldn’t need to read from beginning to end to understand the context.
rules.violation_condition: A narrative’s introduction leaves its context unclear, so users must read through the narrative to understand it.
when: Applies to the introduction of a narrative.
The appropriate way to establish context varies with the content type.
rules.why: The rule-grain test separates an introduction’s adequacy from the mere presence of a beginning, middle and end.

rules.quote: Omit anything that isn’t related to your primary message.
rules.violation_condition: The middle of a narrative contains material unrelated to its primary message.
when: Applies to the middle of a narrative.
Assess relevance against the narrative’s primary message, including relevant supporting material.
rules.why: This is an explicit textual restriction, distinct from the descriptions of what a narrative’s middle can contain.

covers.quote: An effective narrative tells a coherent story.

rules.quote: There must be a logical connection between the 3 parts.
rules.violation_condition: The beginning, middle and end of a narrative are not logically connected.
when: Applies to the relationship between the beginning, middle and end of a narrative.
rules.why: G-4 uses the explicit logical-connection requirement rather than making the description of coherence a second rule.

rules.violation_condition: The parts of a narrative lack headings that signpost the content for users.
when: Applies within the beginning, middle and end of a narrative.
rules.why: The rule-grain test separates signposting with headings from smooth transitions between paragraphs.

rules.quote: Within them, use headings as signposts and paragraphs that flow smoothly from one to the next.
rules.violation_condition: Adjacent paragraphs within a narrative part have abrupt or incoherent transitions.
when: Applies to paragraph-to-paragraph progression within the beginning, middle and end.
This check concerns continuity between paragraphs, not the presence of headings.
rules.why: The rule-grain test splits the sentence’s two independently flaggable properties: heading signposts and paragraph flow.

rules.quote: Users must be able to understand the relationship between any people and events you describe and the design elements you include.
rules.violation_condition: The narrative leaves the relationships among described people, events and included design elements unclear to users.
when: Applies to people and events described in the narrative and to included design elements relevant to those relationships.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the related kinds of entities within one relationship-clarity check.
